## Can Treasuries Still Protect Your Portfolio?


November 24, 2026


When stocks fall, investors often turn to government bonds. Our Global Head of Macro Strategy Matt Hornbach looks at whether the market's favorite hedge has lost its appeal.


## Transcript


**Matthew Hornbach:** Welcome to Thoughts on the Market. I'm Matthew Hornbach, Global Head of Macro Strategy at Morgan Stanley.


Today, can Treasuries once again protect a portfolio when stocks fall?


It's Tuesday, November 24th at 10am in New York.


Last week, the S&P 500 fell every day and closed in correction territory.


Doubts about the AI trade drove most of the selling, and Treasuries rallied even as Fed officials argued for more rate hikes. Ten-year yields fell about a fifth of a percentage point on the week back below 5 percent.


That's what a hedge is supposed to do. For much of the past few years, however, Treasuries fell alongside stocks instead. In our view, Treasuries can work as a hedge again when the worry is about slower growth. When the worry is about inflation, however, bonds and stocks still tend to fall together.


It ultimately comes down to what investors expect the Fed to do next. When inflation is the problem, the Fed raises rates. Bond yields rise, so the prices of existing bonds fall. And higher borrowing costs weigh on stocks too. That's the pattern we saw from 2022 to 2024.


When stocks had a bad week, Treasuries usually had one too. This year, sticky inflation and higher energy prices brought that pattern back.


When growth is the problem, however, it works the other way. Investors expect the Fed to tighten less or eventually to cut. Yields fall, bond prices rise, and Treasuries cushion the loss in stocks.


Last week looked a lot like that. Commodity prices slid. Inflation expectations priced into the bond market came down, and traders scaled back bets on a December rate hike.


The level of yields helps too. The 10-year yield, near 5 percent, already assumes strong growth. Counting inflation, it implies that the economy grows about 5.5 percent a year for a decade. Our economists, though, expect slower growth than that next year, with inflation easing.


For Treasury yields to reach 6 percent, for example, markets would need to price many more Fed rate hikes. That means a policy rate back at the peak of the last cycle. Quite something. Our economists see the Fed stopping after hikes in December and March, so anything but going back to the peak of the last cycle.


If growth really does crack, the payoff in Treasuries is going to be large. In one of our economist scenarios, AI investment falls short. The Fed then cuts deeply in the second half of 2028. In that case, we see 10-year yields near 3.5 percent by the end of next year. That's roughly 1.5 percentage points below our base case.


A move like that helps bond investors. Falling yields lifts the prices of the bonds they already own. With yields near 5 percent, they also collect solid income while they wait.


And it helps borrowers too. Lower 10-year yields tend to pull down mortgage rates, auto loans, and corporate borrowing costs. That makes buying a home or expanding a business more affordable.


For stock investors, holding high-quality bonds alongside stocks should help in a growth scare. Our cross-asset strategists also favor adding stocks while keeping bonds as a hedge.


Of course, our base case has no downturn. We expect 10-year yields to stay near 5 percent through next year, close to current market implied pricing. Treasury returns would come mostly from income in that case.


Currency markets also showed the same demand as Treasuries did last week for safety. The dollar rose, helped by safe haven buying. And on Friday, the yen and the Swiss franc gained too. We expect a modestly stronger dollar next year in our base case as U.S. rates stay above most others. For U.S. investors, a stronger dollar weighs on the value of foreign holdings, but it makes imports and travel abroad cheaper.


We would change our base case view if oil jumped again and inflation stopped cooling. Then, of course, the Fed would have to hike more than our economists expect. Treasuries would likely fall alongside stocks again, as they did earlier this year. Mortgage rates would climb, and both stocks and bonds would lose value.


However, if payrolls and business investments start to fall instead, markets would move towards our downside scenario. Treasuries would then rally just when stock investors need them the most.


So, where does that leave us on this question about Treasuries acting as a hedge to stocks again? We think they can, as long as the scare is slower growth and not higher inflation.


Thanks for listening. If you enjoy Thoughts on the Market, please leave us a review wherever you listen. And share the podcast with a friend or colleague today.


Hosted By


- Matt Hornbach

### [From EVs to Robots: China’s Edge in Physical AI](https://www.morganstanley.com/insights/podcasts/thoughts-on-the-market/china-ai-adoption-real-world-laura-wang-tim-hsiao-sheng-zhong)

## Transcript


**Laura Wang:** Welcome to Thoughts on the Market. I'm Laura Wang, Chief China Equity Strategist at Morgan Stanley Research. And on this very special episode of the podcast, we're coming to you directly from Morgan Stanley's Asia Pacific Summit in Singapore to discuss the physical AI revolution: how China is bringing AI to the real world.


I'm joined by Tim Hsiao, Head of Greater China Auto and Mobility Research, and Sheng Zhong, Head of China Industrial Research. And with that, let's get started.


So, I want to start with Sheng Zhong. So, you covered the robots, the humanoids, all the exciting things, right? I want to understand – because for those things to work, we do not only need the brain. We actually need the components, the parts, the batteries, the motors, the actuators, all to work together.


Do you think that's where China is really differentiated versus the rest of the competitors? And where do you see the biggest gaps that still needs to be closed?


**Sheng Zhong:** We do think China ha\[s\] a unique advantage in the physical AI and also robotics.


It's not only about the frontier AI model, it's more about the manufacturing. It's more about the supply chain.


So, we think China's uniqueness and advantage lies in its vast supply chain and also the application scenarios. So, the supply chain built in the past decades from the smartphone, from the EVs, renewable energy, they can be used in the robotics. And then the robotics, they need \[to\] collect the physical data from their application to the real work scenario.


So, China, I think, ha\[s\] vast working scenarios that can collect the data and then flywheel to the robot development. So, I think that is \[a\] very unique advantage.


We still think the foundation model of embodied AI is also a very important part. And, on this perspective, we think China still ha\[s\] the constraint from the advanced chips and more advanced frontier models.


That is the gap. I think China need\[s\] to catch up and need\[s\] to close more and combine it with the hardware side.


**Laura Wang:** Thanks very much, Sheng. And the next question would be for Tim. Tim, you've covered auto industry for many years, and we understand that in the past, cars are more competing in terms of designs, the driving experience, and the energy efficiency particularly. But now as we enter the physical AI world, what do you think is shifting by introducing this physical AI into the car industry?


**Tim Hsiao:** So, we do think the whole dynamics has been changing because the physical AI, will change the competitive landscape over the next three years. So, I think in China Auto, China EV, bring in physical AI on the road at scale.


So, it combine\[s\] the real-world data you can collect every day. It combine\[s\] the advanced manufacturing. It combine\[s\] the paying customers. So, all this together, basically, can be used or put on the millions of the connected machines that can learn, can sense, can act every day.


In the meantime, I think physical AI also bring in the China EV scaled into a bigger commercial opportunity. Because nowadays, with the AI, I think the car can earn more and the factory can cost less. So, on the road, for example, you look at the smart EVs, the launch over the past few years, they basically combine the sensor computing and also the motion control software. And it's for daily use.


I think a couple years ago, it's basically it's hard to imagine it would happen, but nowadays, you can easily buy older cars in China. So I think, competition-wise, it's no longer about design. I think design is still very important. But beyond that, I think the functionality, technology features and the data, the autonomous driving and the human-machine interface will be getting more importance.


And on the other side, would be the manufacturing. I think the physical AI will basically, help China to make their manufacturing expertise more transferable. Because one of the major reasons is that if you think about what happened to the China auto industry this year, we are looking for the export. The vehicle export to reach nine to 10 million.


So that implies about 50 to 60 percent year-over-year volume increase. But of course, to sustain this kind of growth over time, you can't just simply rely on export. You need to localize the production. So, we do believe that the physical AIs or AI-guided manufacturing could help to – to handle this kind of diverse workforce scale and to minimize the cultural shock. And to improve the efficiency, to improve the quality, and reduce the cost.


So, we do believe that in the future, for the globalization, I think AI will also play a very important role to facilitate, the auto industry's global extension.


**Laura Wang:** So as we walk through 2026, investors actually have all experienced a quick transition or shift of trades from the AI infrastructure to the adoption layer and to the different channels for AI diffusion.


So I think the entire market is looking for where the physical AI or the next AI diffusion channel that can really scale. Do you think intelligent vehicles would be the next largest thing that could happen to AI diffusion? And what would make it work, particularly commercially?


**Tim Hsiao:** I do believe that the auto, especially smart EV, would be one of the key platforms for this kind of physical AI adoptions. One of the major reason is that, each year I think we have around 20 millions the cars sold in China. Probably three years ago, I would say probably just 10 - 15 percent of these were smart EV. But nowadays I would say more than 90 percent of these have the smart features.


So, the majority of the cars, they combine the sensors, combine the computing units, they combine the software, they combine the motion controls; all these kind of smart features, into the car.


More importantly, the thing about the whole usage scenario is not only for the passenger vehicles. But it also empower\[s\] the commercial vehicles for logistic, for the truck, for, for vans.


So, there are actually a lot of opportunity because one of the key debate is that we have the software, we have the technology, but we don't have use case. But in China, we are using that every day.


And we'd expect the penetration to reach 50 percent by 2030.


As we think about one of the hottest topic\[s\] these days – robotaxi. We are looking for 46,000 of robotaxi in China by 2028. And it could achieve; easily achieve one million by 2035.


So, all this together make us believe that we are no longer talking about the transportation. It's become the tech devices and that's one of the major reason\[s\] I'm very confident.


It’s definitely a strong candidate for the physical AI deployment in the upcoming years.


**Laura Wang:** Sheng, I want to bring the discussion back to you. when we think about humanoids, that's very different from cars. \[Be\]cause cars, at the end of the day, still bring people from one point to another point, right? There is a very specific purpose of using cars. But what about humanoids, particularly those are the human-shaped robots.


Robots itself is not a new concept.


But why do we have to be so stuck with this human-shaped robot idea? What better economics can humanoids bring to the table?


**Sheng Zhong:** Yeah. So, basically you see a lot of industrial robot and some moving robot everywhere in the warehouse, in the factories. I think that is increased the productivity greatly already. And this is what people \[are\] always asking. Why \[do\] we still need humanoids? So, if you look at the industrial robot and other robot. They are more worked in the structured environment: in factory, in warehouse, in the ports. But our world is non-structured in most of cases. At your home, at service areas… Then a humanoid that can be a better format in these scenarios, in my view.


So that is why we need humanoid that \[does\] not only assist people/human. But that can do a lot of work instead of human.


**Laura Wang:** So now I want to actually try to bring the robot discussion and the auto discussion together. So, talking about scalability, and if we think about how China has the largest EV fleet in the world.


So how can we think about how the EV industry or the training, the driving, and all the data that's happening on a daily basis can actually help the robot industry? Tim to you.


**Tim Hsiao:** Yeah. Probably I just a kickstart; for scale matters because data matters. So, if you think about the smart EV fleet in China because it's such a huge size of fleet. They will encounter diverse weathers, the driving conditions, the traffic, and driving behaviors.


And that they can help then to collect a lot of different data and quality data that can further help training, inferencing, and validation. For example, one vehicle probably can collect 10 hours useful data.


If you think about the one million cars, we can get probably 36.5 billion useful hours data. And today, I think \[in\] China, there are probably 45 to 50 million NEVs fleet.


And going forward, for now, the majority of the cars are still running on China or in the major cities. But, with the overseas or global expansion, we do believe that a more EV startup or a car maker can bring the smart EV to the overseas market, to collect even more diverse data, which can further enhance the smart mobility.


**Laura Wang:** So, within the auto industry, and when we talk about physical AI, we have privately owned cars, we have commercial fleet, and we have robotaxis.


So, if we think about these three different, sort of, you know, opportunity sets, where do you think the commerciality could first materialize? And why is that?


**Tim Hsiao:** So, in our view, I think hardware component suppliers would be the early beneficiary. Because one of the major reasons, as I just mentioned, to achieve the certain, like a level two, level three, or even like a level four functionality. You would definitely need to have hardware spec ready.


So, like sensors, the lidars, the computing units, you would definitely need to upgrade it first before you can deliver this or achieve a certain functionality. So, we do believe that in the upcoming years, especially in China, I think all the car makers. Basically, they participate in this kind of arm race.


They would definitely keep upgrading the spec of the cars. So, the component size I think will benefit first. But in the mid- to long-term, of course, I think, the NAS can benefit from like a recurring revenue source. Probably they can monetize a service fee, license fee, or even like robotaxi operators that can be the mid- to long-term winners.


But in the next 12 to 18 months, we still believe that the hardware component side will see more meaningful value content upgrade opportunities.


**Laura Wang:** And let's bring that economics discussion to the humanoid space.


Where do you think the most profit will be preserved and kept within the humanoid industry?


**Sheng Zhong:** Yeah. Actually, I think what Tim mentioned for EV had a lot of learnings for humanoid, for robotics as well. So, in humanoid space, I think, it's similar. We also need a supply chain.


The upstream component, they will benefit first.


Because this downstream is very fragmented and diversified. But upstream they have a more consolidated suppliers, and they are benefiting from the scale first.


And then moving forward, the robot will be applied to the real economy. And, in the industry, it's already talking about the token, fees for robot as a possibility, and that maybe we can translate that to a service as well.


So, when the robot applies to the real scenario, the application service is also a profit pool for the industry. And in the end, we think the robot company that own the ecosystem from the robot development and also the application services will enjoy a very good profitability level.


**Laura Wang:** Thank you all for a great discussion.


**Robin Xing:** Thank you.


**Tim Hsiao:** Thank you.


**Laura Wang:** For those at home, if you enjoy Thoughts on the Market, feel free to share with a friend or colleague today.

### [China's Bet on Physical AI](https://www.morganstanley.com/insights/podcasts/thoughts-on-the-market/china-physical-ai-payoff-laura-wang-robin-xing)


Live from Morgan Stanley's Asia Pacific Summit in Singapore, our China Equity Strategist Laura...

## Transcript


**Laura Wang:** Welcome to Thoughts on the Market. I'm Laura Wang, chief China Equity Strategist at Morgan Stanley Research. And on this very special episode of the podcast, we're coming to you directly from Morgan Stanley's Asia Pacific Summit in Singapore to discuss the physical AI revolution, how China is bringing AI to the real world.


I'm joined by Robin Xing, Chief China Economist. Let's get started. So AI's next chapter is not just about what it says to us.


It's about what it can do in the physical world, from vehicles on our roads to robots on factory floors. Our emerging frontiers research points roughly at 12 trillion US dollars of incremental industry 5.0 investment over the next 10 years. Across the broader frontier industries, we actually forecast addressable market to expand from the current 1.4 trillion US dollars to 3.2 trillion by 2030.


And China's manufacturing depth and deployment scale could give it a distinctive advantage. But we all know that more investment is not necessarily more value. We expect the broader productivity payoff to become more visible from 2028. And today, we want to explore what turns smarter machines into better economics, stronger profits, and higher incomes.


So how China can build physical AI and actually make it pay off. So I want to start with the big picture. Much of the AI debate focuses on who builds the best model. When AI moves into the physical world, what changes in the competitive equation, and what do you think will give China an edge?


**Robin Xing:** Thank you, Laura. So phase one of AI revolution is probably some people will call it a chat box helping you writing emails, right? But when we call physical AI, that's the second chapter of AI revolution, is industry-wide adoption of AI. It's AI shifting from just staying in the clouds, going into the real world, factories, ports, logistics, and that could rewire the existing, uh, industry and try to unleash productivity for all these scenarios China is good at.


China is largely a manufacturing-based economy, so simply working from the cloud is not so helpful for their productivity. Instead, they are betting on in the next five years it will be robotics, it would be industrial factories upgrade, it would be these drones and the cars helping them to unleash productivity.


But on its macro impact, I see a two-stage macro equation because at this moment, China still face a bottleneck. That's chips, that's upstream, equipment, semiconductor, GPUs. So they are still investing in these bottleneck enablers, which you call it, picks and shovels. That's booming, but that's only a small portion of the Chinese economy, about low single digit of their total CapEx.


So its contribution to China's potential growth is still limited. But from twenty twenty-eight onwards, we are expecting a series of moments in China's AI computing power, in China's hardware, um, be it a GPU memory or the super pod interconnector, pulling them together to use some engineering innovation to bypass single chip limits.


So that would give China the wider opportunity of using these, using these AI brains into robotics and the industries, upgrading their factories. That's why we do see much broader implication for the economy from twenty twenty-eight onwards, contributing about .3 percentage point in terms of productivity gain.


And the CapEx contribution will also triple from today's investment in those bottlenecks. But in near term, it's still muted in terms of helping China to break out the deflation trap, because right now it's still about investing in upstream bottleneck enablers.


**Laura Wang:** Thanks, Robin. Um, we understand that the investment spending doesn't necessarily take place together with the productivity gains. And as you and I just published our 2027 New Year outlook, we both understand that the Chinese macroeconomy will continue to be challenged by some of the macro concerns.


So when do you think we would start to see some of that real impact on the macroeconomy, and what would need to happen for that to take place?


**Robin Xing:** That's a good question. In the past cycles, China was able to make a lot of, uh, technology progress, winning global market share, but that does not translate to profits for corporates or income for household.


But three structural factors are helping us to break this deflation trap, making this new physical AI investment different from previous cycles. Number one is the nature of investment. Out of this twelve trillion dollar incremental investment in Industry five point zero or physical AI in China, more than half of that will be rewiring existing factories about making them more intelligent, making this, more passive automation into proactive, adaptive production.


And that means, robotic industrial software. The second factor here is policy. Eighty percent of China's industrial policy, this subsidy for capacity, was done by local government in the past.


But since late last year, there has been two initiatives. One is the so-called anti-involution, changing the KPI, the promotion metrics for local authorities. So now the local mayors don't have the mandate to subsidize all these factories. Number two, they are also running out of money given the land revenues rank a lot.


So local government basically reduced the export rebates and also claw back some of these high tech tax privileges for firms. In near term, that's probably negative for certain firms, but over the medium to longer run, that's encouraging firms to consolidate the factories to, not just to keep expanding, but try to keep efficiency and the profit margins.


That's why we think with both policy and the different nature of industry investment, over the next three to five years, the profit margin of industrial firms in China could improve from today's five percent to eight percent.


**Laura Wang:** Robin, as you and I worked, through the, blue paper on emerging frontiers, I think one conclusion we have reached is that the corporate earnings actually can improve ahead of the household effect when the, benefit can trickle down and spill over to household consumption so, um, how do you think about this? When can we and how can we start to see that positive feed into the household consumption?


**Robin Xing:** That's a very good question because Um, robotics, they don't drink latte, they don't wear sneakers, so it's not directly creating consumption demand. And in the past, when China created so much supply, the spill over to household income was limited partially because of excess supply.


So we need to see three things happening before consumers can really benefit from the technology upgrade. One is, investment discipline. The same we mentioned, they have to spend this money on rewiring existing factory, making them more intelligent, cost reduction, more efficient, rather than doing all this greenfield capacity build out to create more redundant, factories.


That's something they need to avoid. Number two is China's housing problem. Part of this weak consumption is due to the deflation triggered by housing adjustment. Recently they have further tightened the rule, which is a negative for growth in near term, but it's also limiting new supply.


And by second half next year, our property team believe housing prices in large cities will stabilize. So the wealth effect channel for consumers will largely normalize. Finally, it's also domestic reform on social welfare. And the Chinese consumers save a lot, partially because the lack of a proper social welfare system for migrant workers and the farmers.


If they can make a pivot towards consumers with a social safety net reform, that's going to really unlock this precautionary saving. So we are looking for these three factors, but twenty twenty-seven is still tough. They are still in a stage of very slowly healing from the balance sheet, be it local government fiscal consolidation, the household deleveraging, and the anti-evolution in near term current CapEx.


But by twenty twenty-eight and onwards, we do believe they may have healed from this balance sheet repair, and that spillover to household income will be stronger onwards.


**Laura Wang:** Thanks very much. Uh, and hopefully partly of that household incomes spillover effect can come from the equity market investment as a opportunity. When we look at how the equity market could potentially benefit from this Industry 5.0 and the frontier, emerging frontier space development, we actually think the earnings growth for Chinese equity market can actually jump from the current 6% on annual basis to above 10% by 2030.


And we actually think the ROE level for investors who invest in Chinese equity market, the ROE can jump from the current 10%-ish level back to above 12%, close to 13% level. So hopefully more investment opportunities and the wealth effect can be created also in the capital market together with the direct effect on household consumption and the wage growth.


Um, Robin, I want to bring this back to you and wrap it up. So, so far we've been talking about all the great changes that's happening within China on technology, on hardware, on software, on deployment in different industries.


How will this change China's role on a global basis?


**Robin Xing:** Yes, that's also an important debate Um, if China is so good at the industrial revolution, it's gaining more market share, will that trigger more geopolitical or trade barriers from other trading partners, and that could, derail China's rise in manufacturing?


Uh, we don't think so, because number one, China is shifting from made in China to made by China. China is working on upgrading with intelligent factories, with more industrial software, the ecosystem. So with that super cycle happening globally on reshoring, on re-industrialization, other countries are also building more and more factories.


But the foreign factories are running based on Chinese components and machinery. That's actually helping China to gain further market share.


But end of the day, China is facing unbalanced growth model. Too much supply, too few consumer demand.


They have to work on domestic reform, on social welfare to rebalance that growth model. That could create more demand opportunity for global firms as well. Only by doing that, I think it could try to manage the trade tensions in a better way.


**Laura Wang:** Thank you for a great discussion.


**Robin Xing:** Thank you.


**Robin Xing:** Thank you.


**Narrator:** That was Part One of a special two part episode from Morgan Stanley's 25th Annual Asia Pacific Summit in Singapore. Join us tomorrow for Part Two of the conversation.
